1: ---
2: name: pc-lib-analyzer
3: description: Analyze a PC open-source software project — a third-party library OR an application — from its git source and produce a single JSON report. Give it a git URL (or a local checkout path) of a Python / C/C++ / Java / JS-TS project. It runs deterministic code metrics, then reasons over the source for function summary, license, dependencies, and low-level/platform API usage, and emits report.json conforming to references/report_schema.json. Designed to be invoked end-to-end (e.g. from an external script or UI via `claude --agent pc-lib-analyzer`).
4: tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Write, Edit
5: ---
6: 
7: You analyze a single PC open-source software project — a **library or an
8: application** — from its source code and output one JSON report. Most of the
9: analysis is **your reasoning over the source** — only code volume is delegated to a
10: script. Be evidence-driven and honest about uncertainty; never invent facts.
11: First decide `library.kind` (library / application / framework / tool / cli /
12: service / plugin): an **application** is launched by an end user (entry points /
13: native launchers / packaging / GUI or CLI), and its app-specific profile goes into
14: existing dims — entry points & packaging → `build_env`, integrated runtime services
15: → `runtime_surface.services`, GUI toolkit & JDK-internal/Attach APIs → `native_api`.
16: This `kind` also selects the dim-9 HarmonyOS口径 (library → 模型 A/B; application → 模型 C).
17: 
18: ## Input
19: A git URL, or a path to a local checkout. Run from the harness project root so
20: the `.claude/skills/...` and `references/...` paths below resolve.
21: 
22: ## Procedure
23: 
24: 1. **Obtain the source.** If given a URL, shallow-clone it **into the project**
25:    (never `/tmp` — see Rules), using the repo name for the dir:
26:    ```bash
27:    git clone --depth 1 <URL> repos/<name>
28:    ```
29:    Note the resolved commit: `git -C repos/<name> rev-parse HEAD`. If given a
30:    local path (e.g. `repos/<name>` already cloned by the runner), use it directly.
31: 
32: 2. **Deterministic metrics (dims 2–4).** Run the code-metrics script and capture
33:    its JSON — these numbers are the source of truth for language breakdown, LOC
34:    (production/test/example), and test counts. Do not recompute them by hand.
35:    Write the output to a path **inside the project** (the same run directory you
36:    will write the report to), never `/tmp`:
37:    ```bash
38:    python3 .claude/skills/code-metrics/scripts/metrics.py --repo repos/<name> --out <runDir>/metrics.json
39:    ```
40: 
41: 2b. **(Optional) Use the codegraph structural index.** When codegraph is enabled the
42:    **server pre-builds the index right after clone** (`codegraph init -i <repoPath>`;
43:    the `.codegraph/` dir lives inside the checkout, gitignored) — so you normally do
44:    NOT need to build it. Just query it (use the exact `<repoPath>` the run prompt gives,
45:    e.g. `repos/<group>/<name>`):
46:    ```bash
47:    codegraph context "<task>" -p <repoPath>
48:    codegraph query <symbol> -p <repoPath> -j
49:    codegraph callers/callees <symbol> -p <repoPath>
50:    ```
51:    Prefer it for the structural lookups in dims 1 and 7. If a codegraph call fails
52:    (index not ready / not installed), fall back to grep/Read and add a `meta.warnings`
53:    note. grep/Read remain the way to read literal text (strings, headers, manifests).
54:    If you ever do need to (re)build it yourself: `codegraph init -i <repoPath>` (first
55:    time) or `codegraph sync <repoPath>` (refresh).
56: 
57: 3. **Reasoned dimensions (1, 5, 6, 7, 8).** For each, read the corresponding skill
58:    file for the full method, then read the actual source to fill in the block:
59:    - Dim 1 function summary → `.claude/skills/function-summary/SKILL.md`
60:    - Dim 5 license → `.claude/skills/license-detect/SKILL.md`
61:    - Dim 6 dependencies → `.claude/skills/dependency-analysis/SKILL.md`
62:    - Dim 7 system & platform API → `.claude/skills/native-api-analysis/SKILL.md`
63:      (classify each group: 标准/特有/系统/ffi/硬件; include managed-language stdlib/system calls)
64:    - Dim 8 runtime & build environment → `.claude/skills/runtime-environment/SKILL.md`
65:      (fills `runtime_surface` + `build_env`)
66:    - Dim 10 capability profile → `.claude/skills/capability-profile/SKILL.md`
67:      (fills `capability_profile`; a SYNTHESIS over dims 1/6/7/8 — do it AFTER those
68:      exist, BEFORE dim 9: flag GUI/3D/媒体/特定硬件 场景 + harmony_status)
69:    Use `Glob`/`Grep`/`Read` to inspect README, manifests, public headers/API, and
70:    representative source files. Prefer breadth on large repos. Cross-check the
71:    script's test framework / language guesses against what you see; refine the
72:    `tests.notes` / `tests.frameworks` if the script was fooled by an odd layout.
73: 
74:    **生产范围（重要，贯穿 dims 1/6/7/8/9）—— 结论只覆盖生产代码，排除测试与示例/演示代码。**
75:    - 读 `metrics.json` 的 `code_metrics.top_dirs`（每个顶层目录的 {dir,code,category}）和
76:      `test_example_dirs` 作为基线：标为 test/example 的目录里的用法**不进结论**。
77:    - 脚本按目录名 token 分类，**会漏判按功能命名的 demo 目录**（如 PyQt 的 `QLabel/`、
78:      `QThread/`、`QAxWidget/` 被记成 production，其实是独立示例）。你要用判断**补判**：当一个
79:      目录其实是独立可运行的示例/教程（README/目录结构指明；或大量并列、各含 `main`/
80:      `if __name__ == "__main__"` 的「按功能命名」目录），按 **example** 处理。
81:    - 只在 test/example 代码里出现的平台 API、依赖、阻碍点**完全排除**，不写进 `native_api` /
82:      `dependencies` / `harmony_adaptation.unadaptable_apis`/`blockers`；每条 evidence 必须来自
83:      生产代码。把范围判断写进 `function_summary`/`harmony_adaptation.notes`，并在
84:      `meta.observations` 记一条（如「将 QLabel/ QThread/ … 判为示例目录，平台 API 据生产代码收敛」）。
85:    - **示例/教程集合**（几乎全是示例、无可安装包、顶层目录基本都是独立 demo）：`function_summary`
86:      如实判为「示例/教程集合，非可发布生产库」；`native_api`/`unadaptable_apis` 据库本体收敛
87:      （通常近空），不把 demo 的 Win32/COM/DLL 当作库的迁移阻碍。
88: 
89: 3a. **Stamp已鸿蒙化 on dependencies (factual, scripted).** After dim 6 dependencies
90:    are listed, find which are already adapted to HarmonyOS PC by checking the
91:    OpenHarmony PC mirror — run the script per ecosystem (it caches; needs network,
92:    skip on failure with a `meta.warnings` note):
93:    ```bash
94:    node scripts/harmony_adapted.js --ecosystem <eco> --names <comma-separated dep names>
95:    ```
96:    It returns `{name:{adapted,source}}`. Set `dependencies[].harmony_adapted` (bool)
97:    and `harmony_adapted_source` from it. Do NOT guess this — it is a factual mirror
98:    lookup. (Alternatively, after writing report.json in step 4, run
99:    `node scripts/harmony_adapted.js --report <runDir>/report.json` to stamp in place —
100:    but doing it BEFORE dim 9 lets the assessment use it.)
101: 
102: 3b. **Synthesis dimension 9 — HarmonyOS PC adaptation.** AFTER the reasoned blocks
103:    above exist, read `.claude/skills/harmony-adaptation/SKILL.md` and fill
104:    `harmony_adaptation` (feasibility / difficulty / path / blockers / effort +
105:    the `porting_class` closed axis — no_adaptation / recompile_only /
106:    needs_adaptation_full（全部可适配）/ needs_adaptation_partial（部分可适配）/ infeasible —
107:    of porting to HarmonyOS NEXT PC) plus, when some functionality is truly unportable,
108:    the API-granular `unadaptable_apis[]` ({api, public_entry, reason, blocking_native_api,
109:    category, evidence} — drives the panel's bottom-up parent roll-up). This is a
110:    **synthesis** pass: do NOT re-scan the source — reason over the already-filled
111:    `library.ecosystem`, `native_api`, `runtime_surface`, `dependencies` (incl. their
112:    `harmony_adapted` flags from 3a — adapted deps are NOT blockers and lower
113:    difficulty/effort), `build_env`, and the dim-10 `capability_profile` (GUI/3D/媒体/硬件
114:    场景 + their harmony_status — a present scenario that is unavailable/specific_hardware
115:    drives a blocker/unadaptable_api), and **reuse their `evidence`**. Also fill
116:    `harmony_adaptation.required_permissions[]` (鸿蒙化后所需 ohos.permission.*, cross-ref
117:    the capability_profile scenario via `source_capability`). Do it inline in
118:    this same session (never spawn a sub-agent). Because dims 6/7/8 are already
119:    production-scoped (see above), `blockers`/`unadaptable_apis` are too — a platform API
120:    seen only in tests/examples is NOT a porting blocker. For an示例/教程集合, converge:
121:    评估库本体（生产代码≈0 时无独立库可移植），不据 demo 定档.
122:    **目标匹配（准确性关键，库与应用通用）**：read `references/harmony-pc-capabilities.json` and match the
123:    project's REQUIRED target capabilities (esp. for apps: GUI toolkit/windowing, JDK
124:    internals like jdk.attach/jvmstat, process/attach model, app delivery形态) against
125:    their target status; emit `harmony_adaptation.target_assumptions[]`. For any
126:    `required` capability whose `target_status` is `unknown`, record the assumption,
127:    **lower `meta.confidence_overall`**, and note it — do NOT assume feasible from
128:    unknown. `available`→no blocker; `partial`→partial blocker; `unavailable`→blocker/
129:    `unadaptable_apis`.
130: 
131: 3c. **Self-check (completeness + cross-dimension consistency).** Before assembling,
132:    re-examine the repo signals (README, manifests, `code_metrics.top_dirs`, codegraph)
133:    and审查每个维度：是否有"本该非空却空"的维度（如有 GUI deps 却空 capability_profile、有
134:    平台 API 却空 native_api）？证据是否到位（关键结论都带 `evidence` file:line）？**跨维是否自洽**——
135:    - `dependencies`/`native_api` 出现 Qt/GTK/SDL/Electron → `capability_profile` 应有 `gui` present；
136:      出现 OpenGL/Vulkan/DirectX → `rendering_3d`；FFmpeg/GStreamer → `media`；CUDA/OpenCL/libusb → `hardware`。
137:    - `capability_profile` 里 present 且 `harmony_status` 为 partial/unavailable 的场景，dim-9 应有对应
138:      `blocker`/`unadaptable_apis`/`target_assumptions`（用 `caused_by`/`source_capability` 交叉引用，**不要重述**）。
139:    - `required_permissions[].source_capability` 必须指向一个 present 场景。
140:    补齐发现的缺口；仍不确定的写入 `meta.observations` 或对应块的 `notes`。这一步与服务端的
141:    `validateReport` 启发式互补（一个是模型推理补全、一个是确定性兜底）。**inline 完成，禁子代理。**
142: 
143: 4. **Assemble `report.json`.** Merge the script fragment (`languages`,
144:    `code_metrics`, `tests`) with your reasoned blocks (`function_summary`,
145:    `license`, `dependencies`, `native_api`, `runtime_surface`, `build_env`,
146:    `capability_profile`, `harmony_adaptation`) and the `library` / `meta` headers.
147:    Conform exactly to `references/report_schema.json`: every top-level key
148:    present, required sub-fields filled. Fill `meta` with `schema_version: "1.0"`,
149:    `analyzer: "pc-lib-analyzer"`, `counter_tool` (from the fragment),
150:    `confidence_overall`, and any `warnings` (carry over `_warnings` from the
151:    fragment). Write it with `Write`.
152: 
153:    Also write `library.ecosystem` using the value you determined in step 3
154:    (function summary). It must be one of: `python`, `java`, `nodejs`, `cpp`,
155:    `rust`, `go`, `dotnet`, `other`. If you are uncertain, use `other`. Write
156:    `library.package_name` (the distribution/package name from the manifest, which
157:    may differ from the repo dir name; `null` if none) — the panel uses it to link
158:    this library into other libraries' dependency trees. When the package name ≠
159:    import name or the library has other known names, also set `library.aliases`
160:    (其它已知名/旧名/CMake find_package 名/Maven groupId:artifactId) and
161:    `library.import_names` (实际 import 名，如 Pillow→PIL) so other libraries' deps
162:    can match it by name. In `dependencies[]`, fill each dep's `source_repo` (上游源码仓 URL,
163:    最强关联键, 尤其当 dep `name` 是别名/接口名如 `find_package(PNG)`→glennrp/libpng) +
164:    `registry_name` when its `name` isn't the canonical package name. Set `library.bindings` —
165:    the languages it provides bindings/wrappers for beyond the core ecosystem
166:    (e.g. C++ core with Python/Java/C# bindings → `["python","java","dotnet"]`; `[]` if none).
167: 
168:    In `native_api`, classify each group by portability — `category`
169:    (标准/平台特有/系统内核/硬件/ffi) + `platform` (windows/posix/linux/macos/portable) —
170:    and drill down with `apis`: per concrete API give name + 中文 purpose + evidence
171:    (file:line) + conditional (#ifdef-guarded). Also
172:    include `dynamic_libraries`: runtime-loaded libraries
173:    (`dlopen`/`LoadLibrary`/`ctypes.CDLL`/`System.loadLibrary`/N-API addons) with
174:    their resolved name, load mechanism, inferred 简体中文 purpose, and evidence.
175:    Emit `[]` if there are none. Manifest-declared deps stay in `dependencies`.
176:    Write `runtime_surface` (network/filesystem/env_vars/subprocess/devices) and
177:    `build_env` (language_standard/runtime_version/build_system/compiler_extensions/
178:    platforms) per the runtime-environment skill — descriptive only, `[]` when empty.
179:    Write `harmony_adaptation` per the harmony-adaptation skill: the closed axes
180:    (`feasibility`/`porting_class`/`effort.person_days`/`blockers[].severity`/`blockers[].adaptability`)
181:    must use schema enum values (`effort.level` is server-derived — don't fill it);
182:    `recommended_path`/`blockers[].category`/`harmony_status` are open
183:    vocab; each blocker carries its `source_dimension` + reused `evidence`.
184: 
185:    For every entry in `dependencies.dependencies`, set `acquisition` (OPEN vocab — coin a
186:    concise value if none of the recommended ones fit), the closed `locality`
187:    (local/remote/system/runtime — set explicitly), `source` (WHERE from), and
188:    `declared_in` (the repo file(s) declaring the integration). This distinguishes
189:    本地/远端/系统 依赖. For non-system, analyzable deps also fill `used_symbols`
190:    (best-effort: the dep's public APIs this library actually calls) — the dim-9
191:    parent roll-up intersects it with the dep's `unadaptable_apis`.
192: 
193:    The output contract (`references/report_schema.json`) is the only hard constraint —
194:    the taxonomies in the skills are recommended starting sets, not closed lists. When
195:    you coin a new value, hit a gap, or face a classification ambiguity, record it in
196:    `meta.observations` (`{dimension, field, kind, value, rationale}`) so it can feed back
197:    into the skills.
198: 
199: 5. **Report back.** The clone stays under `repos/` (it is gitignored). Return the
200:    absolute path to `report.json` plus a concise digest: one-liner, primary
201:    language, ecosystem, production-vs-test LOC, test-case count, license, top
202:    runtime dependencies, and notable native/platform APIs.
203: 
204: ## Rules
205: - The `function_summary` block (summary, category names/descriptions, domain,
206:   target_users) and `library.one_liner` must be written in **简体中文**; keep
207:   proper nouns (SPDX ids, language/dependency names) in their original form.
208: - All files you create — clone, metrics, report, any scratch — must live **inside
209:   the project** (prefer the report's run directory). NEVER write to `/tmp` or any
210:   path outside the project: the headless runner auto-rejects external directories,
211:   which aborts the analysis with no report.
212: - Ground every reasoned claim in something you actually read; cite it in the
213:   `evidence` fields. If evidence is thin, lower the `confidence` and say so.
214: - Keep the script's line/test numbers verbatim; your job is interpretation, not
215:   re-counting.
216: - If a dimension genuinely doesn't apply (e.g. a pure-Python lib with no native
217:   API), emit the empty/cross-platform shape the skill specifies — don't omit the key.
218: - One library per run. Deterministic blocks must match the script output exactly.
219: - **Do the whole analysis yourself in one session — never spawn sub-agents / use a
220:   `task` tool.** Sub-agent sessions don't stream to the run log (the panel goes dark)
221:   and lose cross-dimension context and the codegraph index. For large repos, get
222:   breadth with `codegraph context/query/callers` then targeted `Read`, not by
223:   fanning out into research agents.

Designed to be invoked end-to-end (e.g. from an external script or UI via `claude --agent pc-lib-analyzer`).
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, Write, Edit
---

You analyze a single PC open-source software project — a **library or an
application** — from its source code and output one JSON report. Most of the
analysis is **your reasoning over the source** — only code volume is delegated to a
script. Be evidence-driven and honest about uncertainty; never invent facts.
First decide `library.kind` (library / application / framework / tool / cli /
service / plugin): an **application** is launched by an end user (entry points /
native launchers / packaging / GUI or CLI), and its app-specific profile goes into
existing dims — entry points & packaging → `build_env`, integrated runtime services
→ `runtime_surface.services`, GUI toolkit & JDK-internal/Attach APIs → `native_api`.
This `kind` also selects the dim-9 HarmonyOS口径 (library → 模型 A/B; application → 模型 C).

## Input

13: ```python
14: from mss import MSS
15: 
16: # The simplest use, save a screenshot of the 1st monitor
17: with MSS() as sct:
18:     sct.shot()
19: ```
20: 
21: An ultra-fast cross-platform multiple screenshots module in pure python using ctypes.
22: 
23: - **Python 3.10+**, PEP8 compliant, no dependency, thread-safe;
24: - very basic, it will grab one screenshot by monitor or a screenshot of all monitors and save it to a PNG file;
25: - but you can use PIL and benefit from all its formats (or add yours directly);
26: - integrate well with Numpy and OpenCV;
27: - it could be easily embedded into games and other software which require fast and platform optimized methods to grab screenshots (like AI, Computer Vision);
28: - get the [source code on GitHub](https://github.com/BoboTiG/python-mss);
29: - learn with a [bunch of examples](https://python-mss.readthedocs.io/stable/examples.html);
30: - you can [report a bug](https://github.com/BoboTiG/python-mss/issues);
31: - need some help? Use the tag *python-mss* on [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/python-mss);
32: - and there is a [complete, and beautiful, documentation](https://python-mss.readthedocs.io) :)
33: - **MSS** stands for Multiple ScreenShots;
34: 
35: 
36: ## Installation
37: 
38: You can install it with pip:
39: 
40: ```shell
41: python -m pip install -U --user mss
42: ```
43: 
44: Or you can install it with Conda:
45: 
46: ```shell
47: conda install -c conda-forge python-mss
48: ```
49: 
50: In case of scaling and high DPI issues for external monitors: some packages (e.g. `mouseinfo` / `pyautogui` / `pyscreeze`) incorrectly call `SetProcessDpiAware()` during import process. To prevent that, import `mss` first.

443:     def _merge(screenshot: ScreenShot, cursor: ScreenShot, /) -> ScreenShot:
444:         """Create composite image by blending screenshot and mouse cursor.
445: 
446:         The cursor image should be in straight (not premultiplied) alpha.
447:         """
448:         (cx, cy), (cw, ch) = cursor.pos, cursor.size
449:         (x, y), (w, h) = screenshot.pos, screenshot.size
450: 
451:         cx2, cy2 = cx + cw, cy + ch
452:         x2, y2 = x + w, y + h
453: 
454:         overlap = cx < x2 and cx2 > x and cy < y2 and cy2 > y
455:         if not overlap:
456:             return screenshot
457: 
458:         screen_raw = screenshot._raw  # noqa: SLF001
459:         cursor_raw = cursor.bgra
460: 
461:         cy, cy2 = (cy - y) * 4, (cy2 - y2) * 4
462:         cx, cx2 = (cx - x) * 4, (cx2 - x2) * 4
463:         start_count_y = -cy if cy < 0 else 0
464:         start_count_x = -cx if cx < 0 else 0
465:         stop_count_y = ch * 4 - max(cy2, 0)
466:         stop_count_x = cw * 4 - max(cx2, 0)
467:         rgb = range(3)
468: 
469:         for count_y in range(start_count_y, stop_count_y, 4):
470:             pos_s = (count_y + cy) * w + cx
471:             pos_c = count_y * cw
472: 
473:             for count_x in range(start_count_x, stop_count_x, 4):
474:                 spos = pos_s + count_x
475:                 cpos = pos_c + count_x
476:                 alpha = cursor_raw[cpos + 3]
477: 
478:                 if not alpha:
479:                     continue
480: 
481:                 if alpha == OPAQUE:
482:                     screen_raw[spos : spos + 3] = cursor_raw[cpos : cpos + 3]
483:                 else:
484:                     alpha2 = alpha / 255
485:                     for i in rgb:
486:                         screen_raw[spos + i] = int(cursor_raw[cpos + i] * alpha2 + screen_raw[spos + i] * (1 - alpha2))
487: 
488:         return screenshot

68:         # These iterations and tests don't involve any traffic with the server; it's all stuff that was included in

260: def intern_atom(
261:     xcb_conn: Connection | _Pointer[Connection],
262:     name: str,
263:     *,
264:     only_if_exists: bool = False,
265: ) -> Atom | None:
266:     if name in _PREDEFINED_ATOMS:
267:         return _PREDEFINED_ATOMS[name]
268: 
269:     if isinstance(xcb_conn, _Pointer):
270:         # Dereference the pointer before using the cache.
271:         xcb_conn = xcb_conn.contents
272:     cache_key = addressof(xcb_conn)
273:     if cache_key not in _ATOM_CACHE:
274:         # This can happen if the connection was closed and its cache cleared, but some code still has a reference to
275:         # the connection object.  We could re-create the cache entry, but it's safer to just fail instead of silently
276:         # allowing lookups to succeed when they shouldn't.
277:         msg = "Connection to X server is closed"
278:         raise XError(msg)
279:     if name in _ATOM_CACHE[cache_key]:
280:         return _ATOM_CACHE[cache_key][name]
281: 
282:     # Atom names are required to be Latin-1, per the X protocol spec, although anything that's not in the XPCS (a
283:     # subset of ASCII) is vendor-defined.
284:     name_encoded = name.encode("latin_1", errors="strict")
285:     cookie = LIB.xcb.xcb_intern_atom(xcb_conn, 1 if only_if_exists else 0, len(name_encoded), name_encoded)
286:     atom_as_xid = cookie.reply(xcb_conn).atom
287:     if atom_as_xid.value == 0:
288:         if not only_if_exists:
289:             # This shouldn't be possible.  We at least need to have a path for the type-checker to be happy, though.
290:             msg = f"X server failed to intern atom '{name}'"
291:             raise XError(msg)
292:         # We don't do negative caching, since any app might intern the atom at any time.
293:         return None
294:     atom = Atom(atom_as_xid.value)
295:     _ATOM_CACHE[cache_key][name] = atom
296:     return atom

34: # A quick refresher on why this module spends so much effort on object lifetimes, and how the pieces fit together:
35: #
36: # 1. Shape of XCB replies.
37: #    Each reply that comes back from libxcb is one contiguous allocation that looks like:
38: #       [fixed-size header][optional padding][embedded arrays/lists]
39: #    The protocol spec describes where those trailing lists live, but callers are not expected to compute offsets by
40: #    hand.  Instead, XCB exposes helper functions such as `xcb_setup_pixmap_formats` (returns pointer + length for a
41: #    fixed-size array) or iterator factories for nested variable-length data.  As long as the original reply is still
42: #    allocated, all of the derived pointers remain valid.
43: #
44: # 2. What ctypes does (and does not) track automatically.
45: #    When user code reads `my_struct.foo`, ctypes returns another ctypes object that still refers to memory owned by
46: #    `my_struct`; it does not copy the value.  To keep that relationship alive, ctypes silently sets `_b_base_` on the
47: #    derived object so the garbage collector knows that `my_struct` must stay around.  This mechanism only works when
48: #    ctypes itself materializes the derived object.
49: #
50: # 3. Why XCB accessors break that safety net.
51: #    The XCB helpers we need - `xcb_setup_pixmap_formats`, `xcb_randr_get_screen_resources_crtcs`, etc. - return raw C
52: #    pointers.  ctypes happily converts them to Python objects, but because the conversion went through a plain C
53: #    call, `_b_base_` never gets filled in.  The GC no longer realizes that the derived array depends on the reply, so
54: #    once every direct reference to the reply drops, libc is free to `free()` the allocation.  Any later access
55: #    through the derived pointer becomes undefined behaviour.
56: #
57: # 4. How this module keeps everything safe.
58: #    After every call into an XCB accessor we immediately call `depends_on(child, parent)`.  That helper installs a
59: #    finalizer on `child` whose only job is to keep a reference to `parent`.  No extra work is performed; the callback
60: #    holding the reference is enough to keep the reply alive until the child objects disappear.  Separately, when we
61: #    first receive the reply, we register another finalizer that hands the pointer back to libc once *all* dependants
62: #    have been collected.  As a result, higher-level code can treat these helper functions just like the XCB C API:
63: #    grab the array you need, keep it as long as you like, and trust that it stays valid.
64:

66: def depends_on(subobject: Any, superobject: Any) -> None:
67:     """Make sure that superobject is not GC'd before subobject.
68: 
69:     In XCB, a structure often is allocated with additional trailing
70:     data following it, with special accessors to get pointers to that
71:     extra data.
72: 
73:     In ctypes, if you access a structure field, a pointer value, etc.,
74:     then the outer object won't be garbage collected until after the
75:     inner object.  (This uses the ctypes _b_base_ mechanism.)
76: 
77:     However, when using the XCB accessor functions, you don't get that
78:     guarantee automatically.  Once all references to the outer
79:     structure have dropped, then we will free the memory for it (the
80:     response structures XCB returns have to be freed by us), including
81:     the trailing data.  If there are live references to the trailing
82:     data, then those will become invalid.
83: 
84:     To prevent this, we use depends_on to make sure that the
85:     outer structure is not released before all the references to the
86:     inner objects have been cleared.
87:     """
88:     # The implementation is quite simple.  We create a finalizer on the inner object, with a callback that references
89:     # the outer object.  That ensures that there are live references to the outer object until the references to the
90:     # inner object have been gc'd.  We can't just create a ref, though; it seems that their callbacks will only run if
91:     # the ref itself is still referenced.  We need the extra machinery that finalize provides, which uses an internal
92:     # registry to keep the refs alive.
93:     finalize(subobject, id, superobject)

139: #### Request / response handling
140: #
141: # The following recaps a lot of what's in the xcb-requests(3) man page, with a few notes about what we're doing in
142: # this library.
143: #
144: # In XCB, when you send a request to the server, the function returns immediately.  You don't get back the server's
145: # reply; you get back a "cookie".  (This just holds the sequence number of the request.)  Later, you can use that
146: # cookie to get the reply or error back.
147: #
148: # This lets you fire off requests in rapid succession, and then afterwards check the results.  It also lets you do
149: # other work (like process a screenshot) while a request is in flight (like getting the next screenshot).  This is
150: # asynchronous processing, and is great for performance.
151: #
152: # In this program, we currently don't try to do anything asynchronously, although the design doesn't preclude it.
153: # (You'd add a synchronous=False flag to the entrypoint wrappers below, and not call .check / .reply, but rather just
154: # return the cookie.)
155: #
156: # XCB has two types of requests.  Void requests don't return anything from the server.  These are things like "create
157: # a window".  The typed requests do request information from the server.  These are things like "get a window's size".
158: #
159: # Void requests all return the same type of cookie.  The only thing you can do with the cookie is check to see if you
160: # got an error.
161: #
162: # Typed requests return a call-specific cookie with the same structure.  They are call-specific so they can be
163: # type-checked.  (This is the case in both XCB C and in this library.)
164: #
165: # XCB has a concept of "checked" or "unchecked" request functions.  By default, void requests are unchecked.  For an
166: # unchecked function, XCB doesn't do anything to let you know that the request completed successfully.  If there's an
167: # error, then you need to handle it in your main loop, as a regular event.  We always use the checked versions
168: # instead, so that we can raise an exception at the right place in the code.
169: #
170: # Similarly, typed requests default to checked, but have unchecked versions.  That's just to align their error
171: # handling with the unchecked void functions; you always need to do something with the cookie so you can get the
172: # response.
173: #
174: # As mentioned, we always use the checked requests; that's unlikely to change, since error-checking with unchecked
175: # requests requires control of the event loop.
176: #
177: # Below are wrappers that set up the request / response functions in ctypes, and define the cookie types to do error
178: # handling.

301:         """Wait for and return the server's response.
302: 
303:         The response will be freed (with libc's free) when it, and its
304:         descendents, are no longer referenced.
305: 
306:         If the server indicates an error, an exception is raised
307:         instead.
308:         """
309:         err_p = POINTER(GenericErrorStructure)()
310:         assert self._xcb_reply_func is not None  # noqa: S101
311:         reply_p = self._xcb_reply_func(xcb_conn, self, err_p)
312:         if err_p:
313:             # I think this is always NULL, but we can free it.
314:             if reply_p:
315:                 LIB.c.free(reply_p)
316:             # Copying the error structure is cheap, and makes memory management easier.
317:             err_copy = copy(err_p.contents)
318:             LIB.c.free(err_p)
319:             raise XProtoError(xcb_conn, err_copy)
320:         assert reply_p  # noqa: S101
321: 
322:         # It's not known, at this point, how long the reply structure actually is: there may be trailing data that
323:         # needs to be processed and then freed.  We have to set a finalizer on the reply, so it can be freed when
324:         # Python is done with it.  The whole dependency tree, though, leads back to this object and its finalizer.
325:         # Importantly, reply_void_p does not carry a reference (direct or indirect) to reply_p; that would prevent
326:         # it from ever being freed.
327:         reply_void_p = c_void_p(addressof(reply_p.contents))
328:         finalizer = finalize(reply_p, LIB.c.free, reply_void_p)
329:         finalizer.atexit = False
330:         return reply_p.contents

559: #### Trailing data accessors
560: #
561: # In X11, many replies have the header (the *Reply structures defined above), plus some variable-length data after it.
562: # For instance, XcbScreen includes a list of XcbDepth structures.
563: #
564: # These mostly follow two patterns.
565: #
566: # For objects with a constant size, we get a pointer and length (count), cast to an array, and return the array
567: # contents.  (This doesn't involve copying any data.)
568: #
569: # For objects with a variable size, we use the XCB-provided iterator protocol to iterate over them, and return a
570: # Python list.  (This also doesn't copy any data, but does construct a list.)  To continue the example of how
571: # XcbScreen includes a list of XcbDepth structures: a full XcbDepth is variable-length because it has a variable
572: # number of visuals attached to it.
573: #
574: # These lists with variable element sizes follow a standard pattern:
575: #
576: # * There is an iterator class (such as XcbScreenIterator), based on the type you're iterating over.  This defines a
577: #   data pointer to point to the current object, and a rem counter indicating the remaining number of objects.
578: # * There is a function to advance the iterator (such as xcb_screen_next), based on the type of iterator being
579: #   advanced.
580: # * There is an initializer function (such as xcb_setup_roots_iterator) that takes the container (XcbSetup), and
581: #   returns an iterator (XcbScreenIterator) pointing to the first object in the list.  (This iterator is returned by
582: #   value, so Python can free it normally.)
583: #
584: # The returned structures are actually part of the allocation of the parent pointer: the POINTER(XcbScreen) objects
585: # point to objects that were allocated along with the XcbSetup that we got them from.  That means that it is very
586: # important that the XcbSetup not be freed until the pointers that point into it are freed.
587: 
588: 
589: ### Iteration utility primitives
590: 
591: 
592: def list_from_xcb(iterator_factory: Callable, next_func: Callable, parent: Structure | _Pointer) -> list:
593:     iterator = iterator_factory(parent)
594:     items: list = []
595:     while iterator.rem != 0:
596:         current = iterator.data.contents
597:         # Keep the parent reply alive until consumers drop this entry.
598:         depends_on(current, parent)
599:         items.append(current)
600:         next_func(iterator)
601:     return items
602: 
603: 
604: def array_from_xcb(pointer_func: Callable, length_func: Callable, parent: Structure | _Pointer) -> Array:
605:     pointer = pointer_func(parent)
606:     length = length_func(parent)
607:     if length and not pointer:
608:         msg = "XCB returned a NULL pointer for non-zero data length"
609:         raise ScreenShotError(msg)
610:     array_ptr = cast(pointer, POINTER(pointer._type_ * length))
611:     array = array_ptr.contents
612:     depends_on(array, parent)
613:     return array

392: class MSSImplXlib(MSSImplementation):
393:     """Multiple ScreenShots implementation for GNU/Linux.
394:     It uses intensively the Xlib and its Xrandr extension.
395: 
396:     :param display: Optional keyword argument.
397:         Specifies an X11 display string to connect to.  The default is
398:         taken from the environment variable :envvar:`DISPLAY`.
399:     :type display: str | bytes | None
400: 
401:     .. danger::
402:         The Xlib backend does not have the same multithreading
403:         guarantees as the rest of MSS.  Specifically, the object may
404:         only be used on the thread in which it was created.
405:         Additionally, while rare, using multiple MSS objects in
406:         different threads simultaneously may still cause problems.
407: 
408:     .. seealso::
409:         :py:class:`mss.MSS`
410:             Lists other parameters.
411:     """
412: 
413:     __slots__ = {"_handles", "xfixes", "xlib", "xrandr"}
414: 
415:     def __init__(self, /, display: bytes | str = b"", **kwargs: Any) -> None:
416:         requested_with_cursor = bool(kwargs.pop("with_cursor", False))
417:         effective_with_cursor = requested_with_cursor and bool(_XFIXES)
418:         super().__init__(with_cursor=effective_with_cursor, **kwargs)
419: 
420:         # Available thread-specific variables
421:         self._handles = local()
422:         self._handles.display = None
423:         self._handles.drawable = None
424:         self._handles.original_error_handler = None
425:         self._handles.root = None
426: 
427:         if not display:
428:             try:
429:                 display = os.environ["DISPLAY"].encode("utf-8")
430:             except KeyError:
431:                 msg = "$DISPLAY not set."
432:                 raise ScreenShotError(msg) from None
433: 
434:         if not isinstance(display, bytes):
435:             display = display.encode("utf-8")
436: 
437:         if b":" not in display:
438:             msg = f"Bad display value: {display!r}."
439:             raise ScreenShotError(msg)
440: 
441:         if not _X11:
442:             msg = "No X11 library found."
443:             raise ScreenShotError(msg)
444:         #: :meta private:
445:         self.xlib = cdll.LoadLibrary(_X11)
446: 
447:         if not _XRANDR:
448:             msg = "No Xrandr extension found."
449:             raise ScreenShotError(msg)
450:         #: :meta private:
451:         self.xrandr = cdll.LoadLibrary(_XRANDR)
452: 
453:         if effective_with_cursor:
454:             # MyPy doesn't quite realize that won't be called if _XFIXES is None.
455:             #: :meta private:

458:         self._set_cfunctions()

460:         with _lock:
461:             # Install the error handler to prevent interpreter crashes: any error will raise a ScreenShotError
462:             # exception
463:             self._handles.original_error_handler = self.xlib.XSetErrorHandler(_error_handler)
464: 
465:             self._handles.display = self.xlib.XOpenDisplay(display)
466:             if not self._handles.display:
467:                 msg = f"Unable to open display: {display!r}."
468:                 raise ScreenShotError(msg)
469: 
470:             self._handles.drawable = self._handles.root = self.xlib.XDefaultRootWindow(self._handles.display)
471: 
472:         if not self._is_extension_enabled("RANDR"):
473:             msg = "Xrandr not enabled."
474:             raise ScreenShotError(msg)
475: 
476:     def close(self) -> None:
477:         # Clean-up
478:         if self._handles.display:
479:             with _lock:
480:                 self.xlib.XCloseDisplay(self._handles.display)
481:             self._handles.display = None
482:             self._handles.drawable = None
483:             self._handles.root = None
484: 
485:         # Remove our error handler
486:         if self._handles.original_error_handler:
487:             # It's required when exiting MSS to prevent letting `_error_handler()` as default handler.
488:             # Doing so would crash when using Tk/Tkinter, see issue #220.
489:             # Interesting technical stuff can be found here:
490:             #     https://core.tcl-lang.org/tk/file?name=generic/tkError.c&ci=a527ef995862cb50
491:             #     https://github.com/tcltk/tk/blob/b9cdafd83fe77499ff47fa373ce037aff3ae286a/generic/tkError.c
492:             with _lock:
493:                 self.xlib.XSetErrorHandler(self._handles.original_error_handler)

499:     def _is_extension_enabled(self, name: str, /) -> bool:
500:         """Return True if the given *extension* is enabled on the server."""
501:         major_opcode_return = c_int()
502:         first_event_return = c_int()
503:         first_error_return = c_int()
504: 
505:         try:
506:             with _lock:
507:                 self.xlib.XQueryExtension(
508:                     self._handles.display,
509:                     name.encode("latin1"),
510:                     byref(major_opcode_return),
511:                     byref(first_event_return),
512:                     byref(first_error_return),
513:                 )
514:         except ScreenShotError:
515:             return False
516:         return True

518:     def _set_cfunctions(self) -> None:
519:         """Set all ctypes functions and attach them to attributes."""
520:         cfactory = self._cfactory
521:         attrs = {
522:             "xfixes": getattr(self, "xfixes", None),
523:             "xlib": self.xlib,
524:             "xrandr": self.xrandr,
525:         }
526:         for func, (attr, argtypes, restype) in CFUNCTIONS.items():
527:             with suppress(AttributeError):
528:                 errcheck = None if func == "XSetErrorHandler" else _validate_x11
529:                 cfactory(attrs[attr], func, argtypes, restype, errcheck=errcheck)

531:     def monitors(self) -> Monitors:
532:         """Get positions of monitors."""
533:         display = self._handles.display
534:         int_ = int
535:         xrandr = self.xrandr
536:         monitors = []
537: 
538:         with _lock:
539:             xrandr_major = c_int(0)
540:             xrandr_minor = c_int(0)
541:             xrandr.XRRQueryVersion(display, xrandr_major, xrandr_minor)
542: 
543:             # All monitors
544:             gwa = XWindowAttributes()
545:             self.xlib.XGetWindowAttributes(display, self._handles.root, byref(gwa))
546:             monitors.append(
547:                 {"left": int_(gwa.x), "top": int_(gwa.y), "width": int_(gwa.width), "height": int_(gwa.height)},
548:             )
549: 
550:             # Each monitor
551:             # A simple benchmark calling 10 times those 2 functions:
552:             # XRRGetScreenResources():        0.1755971429956844 s
553:             # XRRGetScreenResourcesCurrent(): 0.0039125580078689 s
554:             # The second is faster by a factor of 44! So try to use it first.
555:             # It doesn't query the monitors for updated information, but it does require the server to support RANDR
556:             # 1.3.  We also make sure the client supports 1.3, by checking for the presence of the function.
557:             if hasattr(xrandr, "XRRGetScreenResourcesCurrent") and (xrandr_major.value, xrandr_minor.value) >= (1, 3):
558:                 mon = xrandr.XRRGetScreenResourcesCurrent(display, self._handles.drawable).contents
559:             else:
560:                 mon = xrandr.XRRGetScreenResources(display, self._handles.drawable).contents
561: 
562:             crtcs = mon.crtcs
563:             for idx in range(mon.ncrtc):
564:                 crtc = xrandr.XRRGetCrtcInfo(display, mon, crtcs[idx]).contents
565:                 if crtc.noutput == 0:
566:                     xrandr.XRRFreeCrtcInfo(crtc)
567:                     continue
568: 
569:                 monitors.append(
570:                     {
571:                         "left": int_(crtc.x),
572:                         "top": int_(crtc.y),
573:                         "width": int_(crtc.width),
574:                         "height": int_(crtc.height),
575:                     },
576:                 )
577:                 xrandr.XRRFreeCrtcInfo(crtc)
578:             xrandr.XRRFreeScreenResources(mon)
579: 
580:         return monitors
581: 
582:     def grab(self, monitor: Monitor, /) -> bytearray:
583:         """Retrieve all pixels from a monitor. Pixels have to be RGB."""
584: 
585:         with _lock:
586:             ximage = self.xlib.XGetImage(
587:                 self._handles.display,
588:                 self._handles.drawable,
589:                 monitor["left"],
590:                 monitor["top"],
591:                 monitor["width"],
592:                 monitor["height"],
593:                 PLAINMASK,
594:                 ZPIXMAP,
595:             )
596: 
597:         try:
598:             bits_per_pixel = ximage.contents.bits_per_pixel
599:             if bits_per_pixel not in SUPPORTED_BITS_PER_PIXELS:
600:                 msg = f"[XImage] bits per pixel value not (yet?) implemented: {bits_per_pixel}."
601:                 raise ScreenShotError(msg)
602: 
603:             raw_data = cast(
604:                 ximage.contents.data,
605:                 POINTER(c_ubyte * monitor["height"] * monitor["width"] * 4),
606:             )
607:             data = bytearray(raw_data.contents)
608:         finally:
609:             # Free
610:             with _lock:
611:                 self.xlib.XDestroyImage(ximage)
612: 
613:         return data
614: 
615:     def cursor(self) -> ScreenShot | None:
616:         """Retrieve all cursor data. Pixels have to be RGB."""
617:         if self.xfixes is None:
618:             return None
619: 
620:         # Read data of cursor/mouse-pointer
621:         with _lock:
622:             ximage = self.xfixes.XFixesGetCursorImage(self._handles.display)
623:         if not (ximage and ximage.contents):
624:             msg = "Cannot read XFixesGetCursorImage()"
625:             raise ScreenShotError(msg)
626: 
627:         cursor_img: XFixesCursorImage = ximage.contents
628:         region = {
629:             "left": cursor_img.x - cursor_img.xhot,
630:             "top": cursor_img.y - cursor_img.yhot,
631:             "width": cursor_img.width,
632:             "height": cursor_img.height,
633:         }
634: 
635:         raw_data = cast(cursor_img.pixels, POINTER(c_ulong * region["height"] * region["width"]))
636:         raw = bytearray(raw_data.contents)
637: 
638:         data = bytearray(region["height"] * region["width"] * 4)
639:         data[3::4] = raw[3::8]
640:         data[2::4] = raw[2::8]
641:         data[1::4] = raw[1::8]
642:         data[::4] = raw[::8]

188:     """Multiple ScreenShots implementation for Microsoft Windows (GDI backend).

190:     This implementation uses CreateDIBSection for direct memory access to pixel data,
191:     which eliminates the need for GetDIBits. The DIB pixel data is written directly
192:     to system-managed memory that we can read from.

195:     constructor parameters.

353:         positive number, while a top-down DIB is specified by setting the height
354:         to a negative number. We use negative height for top-down orientation.
355:         https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/ns-wingdi-bitmapinfoheader

387:                     size = width * height * 4

29: def parse_edid(edid_data: bytes) -> dict:
30:     """Parse a monitor's EDID block.
31: 
32:     Many fields are currently ignored, but may be added in the future.
33: 
34:     If the EDID block cannot be parsed, this returns an empty dict.
35: 
36:     The dict defines the following fields.  Any of these may be
37:     missing, if the EDID block does not define them.
38: 
39:     - id_legacy (str): The legacy monitor ID, used in a number of
40:       APIs.  This is simply f"{manufacturer}{product_code:04X}".
41:       Those subfields are not part of the returned dict, but are
42:       nominally described as:
43: 
44:       - manufacturer (str): A three-letter, all-uppercase code
45:         specifying the manufacturer's legacy PnP ID.  The registry is
46:         managed by UEFI forum.
47:       - product_code (int): A 16-bit product code.  This is typically
48:         displayed as four hex digits if rendered to a string.
49: 
50:     - serial_number (str | int): Serial number of the monitor.  EDID
51:       block may provide this as an int, string, or both; the string
52:       version is preferred.
53:     - manufacture_week (int): The week, 1-54, of manufacture.  This
54:       may not be populated, even if the year is.  (The way the weeks
55:       are numbered is up to the manufacturer.)
56:     - manufacture_year (int): The year, 1990 or later, of manufacture.
57:     - model_year (int): The year, 1990 or later, that the model was
58:       released.  This is used if the manufacturer doesn't want to
59:       update their EDID block each year; the manufacture_year field is
60:       more common.
61:     - display_name (str): The monitor's model.  This is the preferred
62:       value for display.  If this field is not present, then id_legacy
63:       is a distant second.
64: 
65:     Currently, the serial_number and name fields are always in ASCII.
66:     This function doesn't currently try to implement the
67:     internationalization extensions defined in the VESA LS-EXT
68:     standard.  However, we may in the future.
69: 
70:     We also don't currently inspect the extension blocks.  The name
71:     and serial number can be in CTA-861 extension blocks; I'll need to
72:     see how common that is.
73:     """
74:     # See also https://glenwing.github.io/docs/ for a lot of the relevant specs.
75: 
76:     if len(edid_data) < _EDID_BLOCK_LEN:
77:         # Too short
78:         return {}
79: 
80:     # Get the basic identification information from the start of the
81:     # header.  This has been part of EDID for a very long time.
82:     block0 = edid_data[:_EDID_BLOCK_LEN]
83:     if sum(block0) % 256 != 0:
84:         # Checksum failure
85:         return {}
86: 
87:     (
88:         header,
89:         id_manufacturer_msb,
90:         id_manufacturer_lsb,
91:         id_product_code,
92:         id_serial_number,
93:         manufacture_week,
94:         manufacture_year,
95:         _edid_version,
96:         _edid_revision,
97:         _ext_count,
98:     ) = struct.unpack("<8s2BHIBBBB106xBx", block0)
99: 
100:     if header != b"\x00\xff\xff\xff\xff\xff\xff\x00":
101:         # Header incorrect
102:         return {}
103:     id_manufacturer_packed = id_manufacturer_msb << 8 | id_manufacturer_lsb
104:     id_manufacturer = (
105:         chr(((id_manufacturer_packed >> 10) % 32) + 64)
106:         + chr(((id_manufacturer_packed >> 5) % 32) + 64)
107:         + chr((id_manufacturer_packed % 32) + 64)
108:     )
109:     rv: dict[str, int | str] = {
110:         "id_legacy": f"{id_manufacturer}{id_product_code:04X}",
111:     }
112:     if id_serial_number != _EDID_SERIAL_NUMBER_NOT_SET:
113:         rv["serial_number"] = id_serial_number
114:     if manufacture_week == _EDID_MANUFACTURE_WEEK_YEAR_IS_MODEL:
115:         rv["model_year"] = manufacture_year + _EDID_YEAR_BASE
116:     else:
117:         if manufacture_week != _EDID_MANUFACTURE_WEEK_UNKNOWN:
118:             rv["manufacture_week"] = manufacture_week
119:         rv["manufacture_year"] = manufacture_year + _EDID_YEAR_BASE
120: 
121:     # Read the display descriptor definitions, which can have more useful information.
122:     for descr_offset in _EDID_DESCR_OFFSETS:
123:         descr = block0[descr_offset : descr_offset + _EDID_DESCR_LEN]
124:         if any(descr[field_offset] != 0 for field_offset in _EDID_DESCR_ZERO_LOCS):
125:             # Not a display descriptor definition
126:             continue
127:         # Check the tag in descr[3].
128:         # These strings are in ASCII, optionally terminated by \x0A then right-padded with \x20.  In case a
129:         # manufacturer got it a little wrong, we ignore everything after \x0A, and we also strip trailing \x20.  (The
130:         # spec requires the \x0A, but some manufacturers don't follow that.)
131:         if descr[_EDID_DESCR_TAG_LOC] == _EDID_DESCR_TAG_SN:  # Serial number
132:             sn = descr[_EDID_DESCR_STR_LOC]
133:             sn, _, _ = sn.partition(b"\x0a")
134:             sn = sn.rstrip(b" ")
135:             rv["serial_number"] = sn.decode("ascii", errors="replace")
136:         elif descr[_EDID_DESCR_TAG_LOC] == _EDID_DESCR_TAG_NAME:  # Name
137:             name = descr[_EDID_DESCR_STR_LOC]
138:             name, _, _ = name.partition(b"\x0a")
139:             name = name.rstrip(b" ")
140:             rv["display_name"] = name.decode("ascii", errors="replace")
141:

145: def to_png(
146:     data: bytes | memoryview[int], size: tuple[int, int], /, *, level: int = 6, output: Path | str | None = None
147: ) -> bytes | None:
148:     """Dump data to a PNG file.  If `output` is `None`, create no file but return
149:     the whole PNG data.
150: 
151:     :param bytes data: RGBRGB...RGB data.
152:     :param tuple size: The (width, height) pair.
153:     :param int level: PNG compression level (see :py:func:`zlib.compress()` for details).
154:     :param str output: Output file name.
155: 
156:     .. versionadded:: 3.0.0
157: 
158:     .. versionchanged:: 3.2.0
159:        Added the ``level`` keyword argument to control the PNG compression level.
160:     """
161:     pack = struct.pack
162:     crc32 = zlib.crc32
163: 
164:     width, height = size
165:     line = width * 3
166:     png_filter = pack(">B", 0)
167:     scanlines = b"".join([png_filter + data[y * line : y * line + line] for y in range(height)])
168: 
169:     magic = pack(">8B", 137, 80, 78, 71, 13, 10, 26, 10)
170: 
171:     # Header: size, marker, data, CRC32
172:     ihdr = [b"", b"IHDR", b"", b""]
173:     ihdr[2] = pack(">2I5B", width, height, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0)
174:     ihdr[3] = pack(">I", crc32(b"".join(ihdr[1:3])) & 0xFFFFFFFF)
175:     ihdr[0] = pack(">I", len(ihdr[2]))
176: 
177:     # Data: size, marker, data, CRC32
178:     idat = [b"", b"IDAT", zlib.compress(scanlines, level), b""]
179:     idat[3] = pack(">I", crc32(b"".join(idat[1:3])) & 0xFFFFFFFF)
180:     idat[0] = pack(">I", len(idat[2]))
181: 
182:     # Footer: size, marker, None, CRC32
183:     iend = [b"", b"IEND", b"", b""]
184:     iend[3] = pack(">I", crc32(iend[1]) & 0xFFFFFFFF)
185:     iend[0] = pack(">I", len(iend[2]))
186: 
187:     if not output:
188:         # Returns raw bytes of the whole PNG data
189:         return magic + b"".join(ihdr + idat + iend)
190: 
191:     with open(output, "wb") as fileh:  # noqa: PTH123
192:         fileh.write(magic)
193:         fileh.write(b"".join(ihdr))
194:         fileh.write(b"".join(idat))
195:         fileh.write(b"".join(iend))
196: 
197:         # Force write of file to disk
198:         fileh.flush()
199:         os.fsync(fileh.fileno())
200: 
201:     return None

1: """Buffers with Finalizers
2: 
3: This is an implementation of buffer objects with Python finalizers,
4: specific to the needs of MSS.
5: 
6: # Caller Contract
7: 
8: The entry point is `finalizing_buffer`.  This is intended to be called
9: by `MSSImplementation` subclasses.  They provide a buffer (such as a
10: ctypes array or mmap object) and a finalizer, and are given a
11: `memoryview` object.  Once the memoryview is garbage collected, and
12: the consumers downstream of that memoryview have released their views
13: of the buffer, the finalizer will be invoked (with no arguments).
14: 
15: At that time, the `MSSImplementation` may release the buffer, return
16: it to a pool for reuse, etc.
17: 
18: This finalizer may be called at any time, from any thread.  It may be
19: called after the MSSImplementation's `close()` method has been called.
20: Implementations must take care not to invalidate their buffers during
21: `close()`, but rather only after finalization.
22: 
23: The finalizer may also be called before `finalizing_buffer()` returns.
24: This may happen if the implementation needs to make a copy rather than
25: using the originally-provided buffer (which is the case on Python
26: versions prior to 3.12).
27: 
28: (Some more caveats appear at the end of this docstring.)
29: 
30: # Background
31: 
32: The Python buffer protocol lets different objects share underlying
33: memory.  For instance, a NumPy ndarray, a Python bytearray object, and
34: a PyTorch Tensor object can all share the same underlying memory.
35: This allows interoperability between these systems without requiring
36: copies.
37: 
38: Copying ("blitting") all the pixels in a screenshot takes time;
39: copying a 4K (3840x2160) BGRA image can take several milliseconds.  If
40: an application is attempting to operate at 60 FPS, each copy consumes
41: a meaningful fraction of the frame budget.
42: 
43: For a high-performance screenshot library such as MSS, it is therefore
44: important to minimize copies.  Ideally, screenshot data would remain
45: in the buffer originally allocated by the operating system, such as
46: the memory returned by CreateDIBSection on Windows or a shared memory
47: segment on X11.  This approach is commonly called "zero-copy".
48: 
49: Getting the buffer to the user is only half the problem.  MSS also
50: needs to know when the user is finished with the buffer's contents so
51: that the underlying resources can be reused or released.
52: 
53: Most code that uses the buffer protocol is written in C.  Since Python
54: 3.0, the C-level buffer protocol has provided a mechanism for
55: exporters to learn when their buffers are no longer in use.  However,
56: the corresponding Python-level API (which can be used by C consumers)
57: was not added until Python 3.12.
58: 
59: Buffer lifetime is not the same as Python object lifetime.  A user may
60: pass the returned memoryview to NumPy, PIL, PyTorch, or other
61: libraries.  Those libraries may keep the exported buffer alive after
62: the original Python memoryview object is no longer reachable.
63: 
64: Therefore, the lifetime of the returned memoryview object is not a
65: reliable signal that the buffer is no longer in use.  Other objects
66: may still hold references to the buffer after that memoryview has been
67: destroyed.  To know when the buffer can safely be reused or released,
68: MSS relies on the buffer protocol's release mechanism.
69: 
70: The buffer protocol permits a wide variety of consumer behaviors and
71: derived-buffer relationships.  Rather than attempting to model all of
72: those interactions directly, this implementation delegates that
73: complexity to Python's existing buffer-management machinery.
74: 
75: ## Performance note
76: 
77: As a rough reference, copying a 3840x2160 BGRA screenshot on
78: contemporary hardware (Amazon EC2 m8i.large, Intel Xeon 6, DDR5-7200)
79: takes approximately 2.5 ms. At 60 FPS, that is about 15% of the
80: available frame time for a single copy.  These numbers are intended
81: only to provide intuition about the cost of copies; actual performance
82: varies substantially by hardware and memory subsystem.
83: 
84: # Design
85: 
86: The central design decision in this file is that MSS interacts with
87: exactly one downstream buffer consumer: a memoryview.
88: 
89: A memoryview is Python's standard object for representing a buffer.
90: It already implements the reference tracking, buffer export, slicing,
91: and format-conversion behavior required by the buffer protocol.
92: 
93: Notably, memoryview objects do not pass buffer requests upstream to
94: arbitrary exporters.  Once a memoryview has been created, it manages
95: downstream consumers itself.
96: 
97: This means MSS only needs to reason about a single interaction: the
98: interaction between `_FinalizingBufferIntermediate` and the memoryview
99: created from it.
100: 
101: One idea that has been proposed is to attach a weakref finalizer
102: directly to a memoryview object and use that as the signal that the
103: buffer is no longer in use.  Testing has shown that this is not
104: sufficient.  A memoryview Python object may be finalized while
105: downstream consumers still hold active references to the underlying
106: buffer.
107: 
108: To obtain a correct signal, MSS uses the Python-side buffer protocol
109: introduced in Python 3.12 via the `__buffer__` and
110: `__release_buffer__` methods.
111: 
112: An instance of `_FinalizingBufferIntermediate` is created and exactly
113: one memoryview is constructed from it.  That memoryview is returned to
114: the caller.
115: 
116: The memoryview tracks all downstream users of the buffer.  When all of
117: those users have released their references, the memoryview
118: automatically invokes `_FinalizingBufferIntermediate.__release_buffer__`.
119: 
120: That method invokes the caller-provided finalizer, which can release
121: or recycle the underlying storage.
122: 
123: If this implementation appears more indirect than necessary, that
124: indirection is intentional.  It narrows the portion of the buffer
125: protocol that MSS must reason about and test.
126: 
127: # Caveats and Invariants
128: 
129: * The finalizer may run after `MSSImplementation.close()` has been
130:   called.  `close()` must not free, reuse, or otherwise invalidate
131:   buffers that may still be visible to users.
132: 
133: * The finalizer may run at any time and on any thread.  Finalizer code
134:   must therefore be thread-safe and must not assume that it executes
135:   on the thread that created the buffer.
136: 
137: * On Python versions prior to 3.12, `finalizing_buffer()` creates a
138:   copy of the data and invokes the finalizer immediately.  In this
139:   case, the finalizer may run before `finalizing_buffer()` returns.
140: 
141: * `_FinalizingBufferIntermediate` intentionally supports exactly one
142:   buffer request.  This restriction simplifies reasoning about
143:   correctness and should not be removed without carefully considering
144:   the resulting buffer-lifetime semantics.
145: 
146: * `_FinalizingBufferIntermediate` remains reachable through
147:   `memoryview.obj`.  Consumers must treat this as an implementation
148:   detail and must not invoke `__buffer__()` or `__release_buffer__()`
149:   directly.
150: 
151: * Finalizer execution during interpreter shutdown is not guaranteed.
152:   Implementations should not rely on finalizers running during process
153:   termination.
154: """

159: from threading import Lock
160: from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

165:     from typing_extensions import Buffer

167: # You can always use this module, and finalizing_buffer.  This variable is for conditionalizing things like test code or

169: FAST_PATH_AVAILABLE = sys.version_info >= (3, 12)

172: class _FinalizingBufferIntermediate:
173:     """Finalizing buffer class.
174: 
175:     Contrary to the buffer protocol, this class only allows a single
176:     buffer to be created.  This simplifies the implementation and
177:     reasoning.
178: 
179:     The creator must provide a finalizer to ensure that resources are
180:     properly released when the underlying buffer is no longer needed.
181:     This will be invoked, with no arguments, after all the downstream
182:     users, such as NumPy or PIL, have released their references to
183:     the buffer.
184: 
185:     This is only useful on Python 3.12 and later; earlier versions do
186:     not support the __buffer__ and __release_buffer__ methods.
187: 
188:     This class should only be used by the finalizing_buffer function.
189:     It is not appropriate for other uses!
190:     """
191: 
192:     def __init__(self, data: Buffer, finalizer: Callable) -> None:
193:         self._mv: memoryview | None = memoryview(data)
194:         self._finalizer = finalizer
195:         # The remainder of these shouldn't be necessary.  As a consequence of the __buffer__ contract and the
196:         # implementation of finalizing_buffer, only one call to __buffer__ and one call to __release_buffer__ should be
197:         # made, and never simultaneously.  But we still include them out of an abundance of caution.
198:         self._buffer_invoked = False
199:         self._release_invoked = False
200:         self._lock = Lock()
201: 
202:     def __buffer__(self, _flags: int) -> memoryview:
203:         with self._lock:
204:             assert not self._buffer_invoked, "Buffer can only be requested once"  # noqa: S101
205:             self._buffer_invoked = True
206:         assert self._mv is not None, "Buffer has already been released"  # noqa: S101
207:         return self._mv
208: 
209:     def __release_buffer__(self, _buffer: memoryview) -> None:
210:         with self._lock:
211:             assert not self._release_invoked, "Buffer can only be released once"  # noqa: S101
212:             self._release_invoked = True
213:         assert self._mv is not None, "Buffer has already been released"  # noqa: S101
214:         # We need to release the memoryview itself, so that when the finalizer is invoked, the underlying buffer object
215:         # doesn't think there are still exported buffers.  (mmap, for instance, won't close a region with exported
216:         # buffers.)
217:         self._mv.release()
218:         self._mv = None  # Extra-defensive
219:         self._finalizer()
220: 
221: 
222: def finalizing_buffer(data: Buffer, finalizer: Callable) -> memoryview:
223:     """Create a finalizing buffer or a copy depending on Python version.
224: 
225:     The finalizer will be invoked when the buffer is no longer in use,
226:     with a caveat.  This will only track uses downstream of the
227:     returned buffer.  If the input buffer is also used in other
228:     places, those are not accounted for.
229: 
230:     On Python 3.12 and later, this returns a memoryview object that
231:     provides a reusable buffer interface.  On earlier versions, this
232:     returns a copy of the data, and invokes the finalizer immediately
233:     after the copy is made.
234: 
235:     This preserves read/write semantics of the original data: if the
236:     original buffer is read-only, the returned memoryview will be
237:     read-only.
238:     """
239:     if FAST_PATH_AVAILABLE:
240:         # Fast path: we can use the Python 3.12 features
241:         return memoryview(_FinalizingBufferIntermediate(data, finalizer))
242:     # Slow path: copy the data.
243:     with memoryview(data) as mv:
244:         # We create a memoryview of the original data so that we can tell if it's read-only or not.  We can't return
245:         # this memoryview, since we're about to invoke the finalizer to release the buffer it got its data from.
246:         copied_data = bytes(mv) if mv.readonly else bytearray(mv)
247:     finalizer()
248:     # We could return copied_data directly and still have a perfectly fine buffer, but always returning a memoryview
249:     # provides more consistency.
250:     return memoryview(copied_data)

1: ---
2: name: function-summary
3: description: Summarize and classify what a third-party library or application does, by reading its source — README/docs, public API surface, module layout, and key implementation files. Produces a prose summary plus capability categories with evidence. Use for dimension 1 of PC library/application analysis. This is model reasoning, not a script.
4: ---
5: 
6: # Function summary & classification (model-driven)
7: 
8: Decide what the subject *is for* and break its capabilities into categories. This
9: is judgment work — read the source, don't pattern-match keywords.
10: 
11: **先判 `library.kind`（被分析对象是库还是应用）。** 这关系到后续维度（尤其 dim-9 鸿蒙口径）：
12: - `library`：被别的代码以 **API 调用**、经包管理器分发（有 public API / 导出符号 / 包名）。
13: - `application`：被**终端用户启动运行**——有启动器/入口、打包分发、GUI 或 CLI 界面（如 VisualVM
14:   这类桌面工具）。其它：`framework`/`tool`/`cli`/`service`/`plugin`/`other`。信号：有 `main`/
15:   启动器脚本/原生 launcher/打包目标(installer/zip)/品牌化/GUI 工具包 ⇒ 多半是 application。
16: 把判断写进 `library.kind`。**对 application，summary 与 categories 按「终端用户能用它做什么、
17: 有哪些功能模块」描述，而不是当作被调用的 API**（应用通常没有稳定对外 API）。
18: 
19: ## 主旨与原则
20: **输出契约（下方 Output）是唯一硬约束。** 下面的清单与取值是**推荐起点，不是封闭清单** ——
21: 遇到不匹配的场景，尽力归类，必要时**自造一个简洁的小写值**，并写进 `meta.observations`。
22: 方法仅是参考思路，可按仓库实际调整；把推理空间留给自己，只要产出符合契约即可。
23: 
24: ## Evidence to gather (in priority order)
25: 1. **Manifest / package metadata** — the strongest signal for the library's
26:    ecosystem. Look for:
27:    - `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg` → Python
28:    - `pom.xml`, `build.gradle*` → Java
29:    - `package.json` → Node.js
30:    - `Cargo.toml` → Rust
31:    - `go.mod` → Go
32:    - `*.csproj`, `*.fsproj` → .NET
33: 2. **README / docs** — `README*`, `docs/`, project website links, the package
34:    description in `package.json` / `pyproject.toml` / `pom.xml`. This is the
35:    authors' own framing; weight it heavily but verify against code.
36: 3. **Public API surface** — exported symbols: Python `__all__` and top-level
37:    `def`/`class` in package `__init__.py`; C/C++ public headers (`include/`);
38:    Java public classes; JS package `main`/`exports`. The public API reveals the
39:    intended capabilities better than internal files. When codegraph is available
40:    (the agent will tell you), use `codegraph context "<area>" -p repos/<name>` and
41:    `codegraph files -p repos/<name>` to map the symbol/module surface fast; fall
42:    back to grep/Read when it isn't.
43: 4. **Module / directory layout** — top-level dirs often map to feature areas.
44:    借 `metrics.json` 的 `code_metrics.top_dirs` 看结构。
45: 5. **A few key implementation files** — open the largest or most central
46:    production files to confirm what the API actually does.
47: 
48: **描述库本体（生产代码），不要把测试/示例当成库的能力。** 当一个仓库其实是**示例/教程
49: 集合**（无可安装包；顶层目录基本都是按功能命名、各自独立可运行的 demo——如 PyQt 的
50: `QLabel/`/`QThread/`/`QAxWidget/`，外加 `Demo/`/`Test/`），如实说明它是「示例/教程集合，
51: 非可发布生产库」，能力分类围绕「它演示了什么」而非把每个 demo 的平台用法当作库的特性。
52: 
53: ## Determine the ecosystem
54: Before classifying capabilities, decide which ecosystem the library belongs to.
55: Use the manifest signal first; if ambiguous, fall back to the primary language
56: from the code-metrics output. Allowed values are exactly:
57: 
58: | Value    | Meaning |
59: |----------|---------|
60: | `python` | Python package (pip / poetry / setuptools) |
61: | `java`   | Java library / JAR (Maven / Gradle) |
62: | `nodejs` | Node.js / JavaScript package (npm / yarn / pnpm) |
63: | `cpp`    | C or C++ library |
64: | `rust`   | Rust crate |
65: | `go`     | Go module |
66: | `dotnet` | .NET library (C# / F#) |
67: | `other`  | Unclear or none of the above |
68: 
69: Rules:
70: - If multiple manifests exist, prefer the one that declares the primary package.
71: - If the repo is a polyglot binding wrapper (e.g. a Python package wrapping a C
72:   extension), classify by the package's distribution language/ecosystem.
73: - If no manifest is present and the primary language is mixed or unclear, use
74:   `other`.
75: 
76: ## How to classify
77: - Group capabilities into **3–7 categories**, each a coherent feature area
78:   (e.g. "HTTP client", "Connection pooling", "TLS/SSL", "Async I/O").
79: - Each category needs concrete **evidence**: the file(s), module(s) or symbol(s)
80:   that implement it. No evidence → don't claim it.
81: - Identify the **domain** (networking / graphics / ML / crypto / data / GUI / …)
82:   and the **target users** (app developers? other libraries? CLI users?).
83: 
84: ## Output (fills report `function_summary`)
85: ```json
86: {
87:   "summary": "2-4 sentences: what it does and for whom.",
88:   "categories": [
89:     {"name": "...", "description": "...", "evidence": ["src/http/client.py", "Session"]}
90:   ],
91:   "domain": "networking",
92:   "target_users": "Python application developers",
93:   "ecosystem": "python"
94: }
95: ```
96: Also set `library.one_liner` (<=120 chars), `library.ecosystem` (the **core**
97: ecosystem, one of the allowed values above), and `library.package_name` — the
98: **distribution/package name** declared in the manifest (`[project].name` / `name`
99: in `package.json` / Maven `artifactId` / `Cargo.toml` `name`), which may differ
100: from the repo dir name. Set it to `null` if there is no manifest or it is uncertain.
101: 当**包名≠导入名或有别名/旧名**时，再填 `library.aliases`（其它已知名/旧名/CMake `find_package` 名/
102: Maven `groupId:artifactId`）与 `library.import_names`（实际 import 名，如 Pillow→PIL）——这些让本库
103: 被别的库的依赖按名关联上（与 `package_name`/`source_url` 一起构成本库的身份键）。无则省略或 `[]`。
104: 
105: Set `library.bindings` — the languages the library exposes **bindings/wrappers**
106: for beyond its core ecosystem (so a polyglot library isn't shown as single-language).
107: E.g. a C++ core with Boost.Python + SWIG Java/C# bindings → `["python","java","dotnet"]`;
108: a JS package with a WASM/native core → list accordingly. Look for binding dirs/tools
109: (`*.pyx`/`pybind11`/Boost.Python, `*.i` SWIG, JNI `*Wrappers`, N-API, emscripten/CFFI).
110: Use `[]` if it only targets its core ecosystem.
111: 
112: ## Language
113: - Write `summary`, every category `name`/`description`, `domain`, `target_users`,
114:   and `library.one_liner` in **简体中文 (Simplified Chinese)**. Keep proper nouns
115:   (library/API/dependency names, language names) in their original form.
116: 
117: ## Rules
118: - Ground every claim in something you actually read. Never invent features.
119: - If docs and code disagree, trust the code and note it.
120: - If the library is large, sample breadth over depth — cover all top-level areas
121:   rather than fully reading one.
122: 
123: ## 自我发现（反哺）
124: 若发现「推荐取值覆盖不到的新场景(new_value) / 契约或分类的盲区(gap) / 难归类的歧义(ambiguity)」，
125: 追加到顶层 `meta.observations`：`{dimension:"function_summary", field, kind, value, rationale}`，
126: 供面板「模型观察」页人工反哺 skill。
